title: Unit – 1 : Session – 3 : SLO – 2  |  ASCII and parity codes
sections: 1. ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) is a 7-bit code assigning a unique number to each letter, digit and control symbol. It lets any two digital systems exchange text unambiguously, forming the basis of digital communication.
2. Even parity adds a bit so the TOTAL number of 1s (including parity) is even; odd parity makes the total odd. Both detect a single-bit error; they differ only in the target parity convention.
Encoding: each character of the message is converted to its 7-bit ASCII code; a parity bit is computed and appended (MSB) to form an 8-bit frame; frames are transmitted over the noisy link.
Verification: the receiver recounts the 1s in each received frame; if the parity does not match the agreed convention, the frame is flagged as erroneous and retransmission is requested.

Example (even parity): letter 'A' = 65 = 1000001 (two 1s — already even) → parity bit 0 → sent as 01000001. If noise flips one bit to 01000011 (three 1s — odd), the receiver detects the parity violation and rejects the frame.
Special characters — c) Used for punctuation
Even parity — d) Total 1s made even
Parity bit — e) Detects single-bit error

Count of 1s in 1000010 = 2 (already even), so the even-parity bit = 0.
Final 8-bit code with parity as MSB: 0 1000010 = 01000010.
